newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN envoy accuses rebels of massacres in east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UN envoy accuses rebels of massacres in east Zaire.

text.p: A United Nation human rights investigator on Wednesday accused rebels in east Zaire of massacring Rwandan refugees during their push across the region late last year and urged a speedy investigation.

Roberto Garreton said upon his return from a three-day visit to the border town of Goma that Tutsi-led rebels who control a sixth of Zaire had failed to come up with satisfactory answers to allegations of killings, torture and disappearances.

His remarks contradicted reports from journalists covering the fighting in Zaire over the past few weeks who have found ordinary people in both rebel and government-held areas expressing strong support for the insurgents.

At a news conference, Garreton said eyewitness accounts of the number of people killed by the rebels ranged from hundreds to 50,000 and demanded a detailed probe by independent experts to be appointed by the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.
"There were massacres by the rebels. That's for sure. There's an enormous list of allegations of massacres but it is impossible to give numbers," the Chilean investigator said.

Garreton's brief visit to the area has failed to unearth more details of allegations by Zaire's main human rights group, the Association for the Defence of Human Rights in Zaire (Azadho), of large-scale massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees.
Azadho had cited dates, places and witnesses to back charges against rebels and their alleged Rwandan and Ugandan backers.
The U.N. investigator was careful not to describe the killings as genocide -- as Belgium and France, the former colonial powers in the region, have suggested.

East Zaire's tinderbox of rival ethnic groups exploded after the 1994 influx of Rwandan Hutus fled across the border when Rwanda's Hutu government collapsed after launching genocidal attacks against Tutsis in which over half a million people died.

But advances by the rebels, who took up arms last October to topple Zaire's ailing ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, forced 700,000 Rwandan Hutus to return home last year and shifted the balance of power in the region, forcing more than 300,000 refugees and Hutu militiamen to flee deeper into Zaire.

Garreton said he saw three mass graves near the empty refugee camps of Kibumba, Katale and Kilimanyako but that his attempts to visit several others had been thwarted by rebels on the grounds of security risks or lack of official authorisation.
In Goma, Garreton said he met a senior aide to rebel leader Laurent Kabila, his chief of cabinet Moese Nyarugabo, who told him that "this is a war and in a war there are killings and disappearances."
"His response was not encouraging," Garreton said. "He told me he couldn't give me an escort to visit a mass grave site because it was Easter holiday."
Zaire accuses Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army and Ugandan troops of supporting the rebels, but they deny these charges.

Garreton said: "I can't say that the Rwandan and Ugandan armies are there with their generals and colonels. But the local people view the rebel forces as an occupation army. It is clear that these rebels are not Zaireans."
